span.label: critique
span.quote: The central argument advanced here is that philosophy of science is best understood not as a search for one timeless criterion of scientific rationality, but as an inquiry into how multiple epistemic ideals—explanation, empirical adequacy, objectivity, progress, and ontological commitment—are coordinated, contested, and reinterpreted within changing scientific practices.

span.label: scientific explanation and theory change
span.quote: This article examines scientific explanation, theory change, and epistemic boundaries in contemporary philosophy of science.

span.label: review
span.quote: The philosophical history surveyed in this article shows that no simple answer has survived intact.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Objectivity is produced, not presupposed: structuring methods and communities so that criticism, transparency and diverse perspectives circulate prevents any single bias or standpoint from going unchecked, which is what makes objective claims possible in a socially organised practice
span.quote: It is what becomes possible when social and methodological arrangements are structured so that no single bias or perspective can easily dominate unchecked.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Realist commitment survives theory change because what is carried across revolutions is the structural content of superseded theories — their relational organisation, mathematical form and dependency patterns — rather than their full ontology
span.quote: If older successful theories were later rejected, perhaps what survives across scientific revolutions is not the full ontology of those theories but their structural content: the relational organization, mathematical form, or dependency patterns they captured.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The pluralisation of explanation was driven by the demand for rigour itself: holding accounts answerable to actual scientific practice forced the abandonment of a single universal schema
span.quote: This transformation did not occur because philosophers lost interest in rigor. It occurred because rigor itself required closer responsiveness to the sciences.

span.label: The account of what a term means is taken from an encyclopedia entry rather than from the literature the entry summarises.
span.note: what this limits: any position attributed here to the incommensurability literature: it is reported from the Stanford Encyclopedia entry on incommensurability rather than from the primary sources that entry summarises
span.quote: The SEP entry on incommensurability clarifies that the term originally referred to lack of common measure and that later philosophical discussion distinguished conceptual and methodological incommensurability

span.label: The paper reports that competing theories may have no shared standard by which to compare them.
span.note: what this limits: any comparison of two theories drawn from this article: it reports the Kuhnian picture as implying competing theories may not always be assessable by a single neutral metric
span.quote: This matters because the Kuhnian picture implies that competing theories may not always be assessable by a single neutral metric

span.label: Carrying a result from a model to the thing modelled is stated not to be automatic, even in the easiest case.
span.note: what this limits: any inference from a scientific model to its target: the article reports that even scale models are faithful only in restricted respects and that translating knowledge from a model to its target is not automatic
span.quote: The models entry notes explicitly that even scale models, which look like the most straightforward cases of faithful representation, are only faithful in restricted respects and that translating knowledge from a model to its target is not automatic

span.label: One of the paper's central terms is reported to name several distinct problems rather than one.
span.note: what this limits: the notion of representation as used in this article: it is reported that no single problem of representation exists and that there are instead multiple distinct issues
span.quote: The representation entry likewise emphasizes that no single problem of representation exists; instead, there are multiple distinct issues about how scientific representations support inference to their targets

span.label: scientific explanation
span.quote: Among the enduring questions of the field, scientific explanation has long occupied a privileged place

span.label: deductive-nomological model
span.quote: modern discussion begins with the deductive-nomological model and its effort to analyze explanation in terms of lawful derivation

span.label: incommensurability
span.quote: The SEP entry on incommensurability clarifies that the term originally referred to lack of common measure and that later philosophical discussion distinguished conceptual and methodological incommensurability.

span.label: scientific realism
span.quote: This historical turn had profound consequences for debates about realism and antirealism

span.label: theory change
span.quote: The SEP entry on realism and theory change frames exactly this challenge, noting that the history of science is often invoked against realist epistemic optimism because once successful theories have later been abandoned

span.label: Mechanistic accounts
span.quote: Mechanistic accounts respond by focusing less on intertheoretic deduction and more on organized constitution and causal production

span.label: unificationist accounts
span.quote: unificationist accounts remained compelling because successful science often explains by showing that apparently different phenomena are manifestations of a smaller set of patterns or principles

span.label: pragmatic accounts of explanation
span.quote: A further complication is introduced by pragmatic accounts of explanation, especially those associated with Bas van Fraassen. The SEP archive on twentieth-century scientific explanation notes that one influential pragmatic line is connected with constructive empiricism and the view that the aim of science is empirical adequacy rather than literal truth about unobservables. On such views, explanation is not assessed solely by metaphysical correspondence or causal revelation, but also by its role within inquiry and its adequacy relative to explanatory interests

span.label: explanatory pluralism
span.quote: Contemporary philosophy of science therefore rarely resolves the issue by simple victory of one model over all others. Instead, it treats explanatory pluralism as increasingly unavoidable, especially across disciplines with different explanatory targets and methods

span.label: underdetermination
span.quote: The problem of underdetermination adds a further boundary question. The SEP entry on underdetermination states the core idea succinctly: the evidence available at a given time may be insufficient to determine what beliefs we should adopt

span.label: Constructive empiricism
span.quote: Constructive empiricism offers a more radical restraint. The SEP entry devoted to it states van Fraassen’s core thesis plainly: science aims to give us theories that are empirically adequate, and acceptance of a theory involves belief only that it is empirically adequate. On this view, the success of science does not entitle us to belief in the literal truth of claims about unobservables. It entitles us only to belief that the theory saves the observable phenomena correctly

span.label: Structural realism
span.quote: Structural realism, for example, has been defended partly as a response to historical turnover by suggesting that what science preserves more reliably across theory change may be structural content rather than the full ontology of earlier theories. The SEP entry on structural realism reflects this by presenting structural realism as a major attempt to retain realist commitment while responding to antirealist and historicist concerns

span.label: empirical adequacy
span.quote: constructive empiricism, as summarized in the SEP entry devoted to it, can hold that the aim of science is empirical adequacy rather than truth about unobservables

span.label: truth about unobservables
span.quote: constructive empiricism, as summarized in the SEP entry devoted to it, can hold that the aim of science is empirical adequacy rather than truth about unobservables

span.label: structural content
span.quote: Structural realism, for example, has been defended partly as a response to historical turnover by suggesting that what science preserves more reliably across theory change may be structural content rather than the full ontology of earlier theories

span.label: full ontology
span.quote: Structural realism, for example, has been defended partly as a response to historical turnover by suggesting that what science preserves more reliably across theory change may be structural content rather than the full ontology of earlier theories

span.label: objectivity
span.quote: objectivity is therefore more subtle than older accounts assumed. The SEP entry on scientific objectivity states that objectivity is an ideal according to which scientific claims, methods, and results should not be influenced by particular perspectives, values, or biases. Yet the same entry makes clear that objectivity applies to many aspects of science and cannot be reduced to a single formula. This is philosophically important because once observation is acknowledged as theory-laden and scientific change as historically deep, objectivity can no longer plausibly mean total absence of perspective. It must instead be reinterpreted as a disciplined achievement of scientific communities, methods, and practices

span.label: elimination of all values and perspectives
span.term: elimination of all values and perspectives
span.quote: What contemporary philosophy of science increasingly concludes is that objectivity must be defended in a richer form: not as the elimination of all values and perspectives, but as the disciplined management of their influence through transparent methods, structured criticism, community standards, and responsiveness to empirical resistance

span.label: Constructive empiricism → empirical adequacy
span.note: Constructive empiricism limits theory acceptance to belief in empirical adequacy. This epistemic-standard relation is not is-a, part-of, same-as, distinct-from, contrasted-with, operationalised-as, causes, or renamed-across-fields.
span.quote: Constructive empiricism offers a more radical restraint. The SEP entry devoted to it states van Fraassen’s core thesis plainly: science aims to give us theories that are empirically adequate, and acceptance of a theory involves belief only that it is empirically adequate. On this view, the success of science does not entitle us to belief in the literal truth of claims about unobservables. It entitles us only to belief that the theory saves the observable phenomena correctly

span.label: Structural realism → structural content
span.note: Structural realism identifies structural content as what may be preserved across theory change. Preservation-across-change is not is-a, part-of, same-as, distinct-from, contrasted-with, operationalised-as, causes, or renamed-across-fields.
span.quote: Structural realism, for example, has been defended partly as a response to historical turnover by suggesting that what science preserves more reliably across theory change may be structural content rather than the full ontology of earlier theories. The SEP entry on structural realism reflects this by presenting structural realism as a major attempt to retain realist commitment while responding to antirealist and historicist concerns

span.label: incommensurability - A CHANGED MEANING THAT THEN SPLIT IN TWO: originally lack of common measure, and later divided by philosophical discussion into conceptual and methodological incommensurability, so the word names an older idea and two newer ones at once
span.quote: The SEP entry on incommensurability clarifies that the term originally referred to lack of common measure and that later philosophical discussion distinguished conceptual and methodological incommensurability

span.label: explanation - SEVERAL MODELS, EACH PRESUPPOSING A DIFFERENT IMAGE OF SCIENCE: discussion begins with lawful derivation and later adds causal, mechanistic, unificationist and pragmatic alternatives, and the article says the sequence matters because the models are not interchangeable accounts of one thing
span.quote: modern discussion begins with the deductive-nomological model and its effort to analyze explanation in terms of lawful derivation, but later developments introduced causal, mechanistic, unificationist, and pragmatic alternatives. This historical sequence matters because each model of explanation presupposes a different image of science itself

span.label: representation - NOT ONE PROBLEM BUT SEVERAL: the article reports that no single problem of representation exists, so a claim that a model represents its target is selective, purpose-relative and mediated by inference rather than a single relation
span.quote: The representation entry likewise emphasizes that no single problem of representation exists; instead, there are multiple distinct issues about how scientific representations support inference to their targets. These observations have far-reaching consequences. They imply that the representational success of science is selective, purposerelative, and inferentially mediated

span.label: Mechanistic accounts - explain through organized constitution and causal production
span.quote: Mechanistic accounts respond by focusing less on intertheoretic deduction and more on organized constitution and causal production

span.label: Unificationist accounts - explain apparently different phenomena through a smaller set of patterns or principles
span.quote: unificationist accounts remained compelling because successful science often explains by showing that apparently different phenomena are manifestations of a smaller set of patterns or principles

span.label: Pragmatic accounts of explanation - evaluate explanations relative to inquiry roles and explanatory interests
span.quote: A further complication is introduced by pragmatic accounts of explanation, especially those associated with Bas van Fraassen. The SEP archive on twentieth-century scientific explanation notes that one influential pragmatic line is connected with constructive empiricism and the view that the aim of science is empirical adequacy rather than literal truth about unobservables. On such views, explanation is not assessed solely by metaphysical correspondence or causal revelation, but also by its role within inquiry and its adequacy relative to explanatory interests

span.label: Explanatory pluralism - multiple models remain necessary across disciplines with different targets and methods
span.quote: Contemporary philosophy of science therefore rarely resolves the issue by simple victory of one model over all others. Instead, it treats explanatory pluralism as increasingly unavoidable, especially across disciplines with different explanatory targets and methods

span.label: Underdetermination - the evidence at a time may not determine which beliefs to adopt

The SEP entry devoted to it states van Fraassen’s core thesis plainly: science aims to give us theories that are empirically adequate, and acceptance of a theory involves belief only that it is empirically adequate. On this view, the success of science does not entitle us to belief in the literal truth of claims about unobservables. It entitles us only to belief that the theory saves the observable phenomena correctly

span.label: Structural realism - preserves realist commitment by privileging structural continuity over full ontology
span.quote: Structural realism, for example, has been defended partly as a response to historical turnover by suggesting that what science preserves more reliably across theory change may be structural content rather than the full ontology of earlier theories. The SEP entry on structural realism reflects this by presenting structural realism as a major attempt to retain realist commitment while responding to antirealist and historicist concerns

span.label: Empirical adequacy - the scientific aim constructive empiricism endorses
span.quote: constructive empiricism, as summarized in the SEP entry devoted to it, can hold that the aim of science is empirical adequacy rather than truth about unobservables

span.label: Truth about unobservables - the aim constructive empiricism contrasts with empirical adequacy

span.label: Structural content - what may survive historical theory change more reliably than ontology
span.quote: Structural realism, for example, has been defended partly as a response to historical turnover by suggesting that what science preserves more reliably across theory change may be structural content rather than the full ontology of earlier theories

span.label: Objectivity - a disciplined communal and methodological achievement, not perspective-free access
span.quote: objectivity is therefore more subtle than older accounts assumed. The SEP entry on scientific objectivity states that objectivity is an ideal according to which scientific claims, methods, and results should not be influenced by particular perspectives, values, or biases. Yet the same entry makes clear that objectivity applies to many aspects of science and cannot be reduced to a single formula. This is philosophically important because once observation is acknowledged as theory-laden and scientific change as historically deep, objectivity can no longer plausibly mean total absence of perspective. It must instead be reinterpreted as a disciplined achievement of scientific communities, methods, and practices

span.label: Elimination of all values and perspectives - explicitly rejected as the richer meaning of objectivity
span.quote: What contemporary philosophy of science increasingly concludes is that objectivity must be defended in a richer form: not as the elimination of all values and perspectives, but as the disciplined management of their influence through transparent methods, structured criticism, community standards, and responsiveness to empirical resistance

span.label: builds-on → Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entries on scientific realism and scientific objectivity
span.quote: The Stanford Encyclopedia entry on scientific realism makes this point directly by observing that debates about realism are connected to almost everything else in philosophy of science because they concern the very nature of scientific knowledge, while the entry on scientific objectivity similarly treats objectivity as an ideal that underwrites the authority of science in society.

span.label: The article's central claim is that philosophy of science should be read not as a hunt for one timeless criterion of rationality but as the study of how explanation, empirical adequacy, objectivity, progress and ontological commitment are coordinated and contested within changing scientific practice.
span.quote: The central argument advanced here is that philosophy of science is best understood not as a search for one timeless criterion of scientific rationality, but as an inquiry into how multiple epistemic ideals—explanation, empirical adequacy, objectivity, progress, and ontological commitment—are coordinated, contested, and reinterpreted within changing scientific practices.

span.label: Epistemic boundaries in science are neither arbitrary nor permanent: they are negotiated limits shaped by explanatory ideals, representational practice, historical change, social organisation and domain-specific standards of success.
span.quote: The contemporary discussions surveyed in earlier blocks instead suggest that epistemic boundaries are negotiated limits.

span.label: Explanation is best treated as a family of related epistemic achievements — lawful derivation, causal-mechanistic production, unification, empirical adequacy and pragmatic usefulness — rather than as one formal relation.
span.quote: Contemporary philosophy of science increasingly treats explanation as a family of related epistemic achievements rather than a single formal relation.

span.label: Realism, objectivity and progress can still be defended, but only in reconstructed form: realism becomes selective and model-sensitive, objectivity becomes procedural, social and critical, and progress becomes multi-dimensional rather than cumulative.
span.quote: Realism becomes more selective and model-sensitive. Objectivity becomes procedural, social, and critical rather than purely perspective-free. Progress becomes multi-dimensional and historically informed rather than simply cumulative.

span.label: Progress should be measured along several dimensions at once — empirical adequacy, explanatory reach, conceptual articulation, representational power, intervention, and critical self-correction — which need not advance together.
span.quote: Science can progress in empirical adequacy, in explanatory reach, in conceptual articulation, in representational power, in manipulation and intervention, and in critical self-correction, even if these dimensions do not always move together.

span.label: The article's twofold conclusion is that monistic images of science misdescribe the heterogeneity of its models, methods and history, and that this heterogeneity nevertheless does not license epistemic despair about scientific authority.
span.quote: First, science should not be philosophically understood through monistic images that ignore the heterogeneity of models, methods, and historical development. Second, this heterogeneity does not entail epistemic despair.

span.label: Because observation is never fully independent of theoretical commitment, explanation cannot be modelled as a one-way derivation from pure data but must be understood as organising phenomena within conceptual frameworks that themselves need assessment.
span.quote: If observation is never entirely independent of theoretical commitments, then explanation cannot be understood as a simple one-way derivation from pure empirical givens.

span.label: The article characterises the resulting stance of the field as fallibilist without cynicism, historically informed without anti-rationalism, and pluralist without indiscriminateness.
span.quote: Its characteristic posture is fallibilist but not cynical, historically informed but not anti-rational, pluralist but not indiscriminate.

span.label: scientific realism
span.quote: The contemporary SEP entry on scientific realism defines realism as a positive epistemic attitude toward the content of our best theories and models, recommending belief in both observable and unobservable aspects of the world described by the sciences.

span.label: constructive empiricism
span.quote: Constructive empiricism offers a more radical restraint. The SEP entry devoted to it states van Fraassen’s core thesis plainly: science aims to give us theories that are empirically adequate, and acceptance of a theory involves belief only that it is empirically adequate.

span.label: underdetermination
span.quote: The SEP entry on underdetermination states the core idea succinctly: the evidence available at a given time may be insufficient to determine what beliefs we should adopt.

span.label: scientific objectivity
span.quote: The SEP entry on scientific objectivity states that objectivity is an ideal according to which scientific claims, methods, and results should not be influenced by particular perspectives, values, or biases.

span.label: incommensurability
span.quote: The SEP entry on incommensurability clarifies that the term originally referred to lack of common measure and that later philosophical discussion distinguished conceptual and methodological incommensurability.

span.label: scientific progress
span.quote: The SEP entry on scientific progress defines progress as result-oriented, concerning success relative to some goal, and explicitly distinguishes it from quality in scientific work.

span.label: scientific pluralism
span.quote: The SEP entry on scientific pluralism states that plurality is now often treated not as a defect to be overcome but as a productive feature of successful science.

span.label: syntactic, semantic and pragmatic views of theory structure
span.term: syntactic, semantic and pragmatic views of theory structure
span.quote: The SEP entry on the structure of scientific theories distinguishes three major families of views: the syntactic view, the semantic view, and the pragmatic view.

span.label: covering-law / deductive-nomological model of explanation
span.quote: The basic intuition of that model is that to explain an event is to show that it was to be expected given general laws and initial conditions.
